title: Food Sources of Early Native Americans

paragraphs.text: It is commonly believed that the first Native Americans traveled from the Old World of Europe into the New World of North America about 15,000 years ago, crossing a land bridge connecting what are now Siberia and Alaska. But this land link disappeared shortly thereafter. Although it is impossible to know for certain how, when, or why the ancestors of the Native Americans first appeared in North America, it seems that either they brought no animals or plants with them, or that none survived. But, by 1492, when the explorer Christopher Columbus first entered the New World, the Native Americans living there were relying on foods that were native to the region.

When the Europeans arrived, there were numerous regional tribes with very different diets, customs and languages throughout the Americas, but many of the foods had spread among the regions due to well-organized trade routes. Trade was facilitated in part by hand signs that became a common way to communicate among several tribes. The wealth of foods in North America made possible a highly satisfying diet. For instance, many of the berries that are popular today for their medicinal properties were also valuable additions to Native American meals; they included blueberries, chokeberries and cranberries.

Animal foods were also a major part of the Native American diet. When humans first arrived in North America, they appear to have been hunter-gatherers who managed to subsist on the plentiful wildlife of this new territory. Large animals such as mastodon – a large, extinct, elephant-like mammal – were an important food source. However, the extinction of such large animals about 10,000-12,000 years ago is believed to have brought about major transformations in the vegetation as well as the animal life of North America. It likely caused many Native American tribes to at least partially rely on agriculture as a main food supply.

One of the best early records of Native American customs and culture was published by James Adair, an immigrant from Ireland. He composed detailed accounts of Native American life as he worked and lived with the original inhabitants of what is now the southeastern USA, from about 1735 to 1790. He later returned home to both acclaim and controversy in Europe. Adair's book included descriptions of the hunting of deer and bears, and the methods of fishing.

In terms of food collection, the early Native Americans were all hunter-gatherers, living off the many plants and animals they found around them. Because they remained a largely Stone Age culture until Europeans arrived with metal tools, little evidence exists of the early cultures other than stone tools and occasional bone fragments from hunted animals. Most of their creations were composed of perishable materials such as wood and animal skins that had disappeared before becoming available to archaeologists. But it is known that Native Americans were masters of surviving with only the most basic tools and starting fires out of sticks whenever the need to cook arose.

Corn, beans and squash – commonly called 'the three sisters' – were central to Native American farming and were always grown together. Of the three, only squash was of North American origin. Corn and beans probably originated in South America, but their use spread throughout North and South America. Corn was the most important staple food grown by Native Americans, and its stalks also could be used as a pole for beans to climb, while its shade benefited squash that grew under the leaves. The beans, as with all legumes, provided nitrogen for the cornd squash. Th ane shade from large squash and pumpkin leaves helped to hold moisture in the ground for all three plants.

In terms of hunting, when Europeans first arrived, the weapon of choice for Native Americans was the bow and arrow, made mostly of wood but occasionally of materials like animal horn. However, the spear had been used initially, long before the bow and arrow, and was enhanced by a sling-like throwing tool called the atlatl. The atlatl, though not as accurate, made weapons more powerful, so it would have been especially helpful in hunting large animals like the buffalo. The bow and arrow, however, would have been best for hunting deer, turkey and most other animals hunted for food.

Early Native American hunters are recognized for their sophistication. They generally prized animals with comparatively large stores of fat and could identify these by their large curves and shinier coats. They knew which animals would be in prime condition at any given time of year, and for this reason, for example, tended to hunt buffalo only in the summer.

Fishing also appears to have been a major source of food for most Native Americans. Most villages were located near a river or large stream where there was a dependable supply of fish and waterfowl. The fishermen used nets and spears, and tended to form large groups to carry out their expeditions for a communal experience that was certain to yield plenty.
In these ways, Native Americans were able to adapt to their natural surroundings to access local food sources.
